messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Very large map distance between markers
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Very large map distance between markers
messages.body_plain:
We estimate the recombination fractions between markers and then convert them to centiMorgans with a map function, and so if the spacing is large it must be that the estimated recombination fraction is close to 0.5.

The estimated recombination fractions are not the same as what you'd get from looking at pairs of markers in isolation, as from est.rf(). The est.map() function uses the full data of markers along a chromosome ("multipoint").

karl

messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Percentange of phenotypic variance explained.
messages.body_plain:
The only function in R/qtl that provides an estimated percent variance explained by a QTL is fitqtl(). But this cannot be used with a non-parametric mapping method.

Here's an example using Haley-Knott regression:

data(fake.f2)
fake.f2 <- calc.genoprob(fake.f2, step=1)
out <- scanone(fake.f2, method="hk")
max(out)

qtl <- makeqtl(fake.f2, chr=13, pos=28, what="prob")
out.fitqtl <- fitqtl(fake.f2, qtl=qtl, method="hk")
summary(out.fitqtl)

karl

messages.subject: GWERk Permutations
messages.subject_clean: GWERk Permutations
messages.body_plain:
Hi Karl et al.
I have been working to implement a permutation method following Chen and Storey (2005) (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1569719/) for my eQTL dataset.
The premise is as follows: if we see differential expression in previous experiments, it is likely due to the presence of ≥ 1 QTL. Given knowledge of the existence of a QTL, our Null Hypothesis is no longer nQTL = 0. Therefore, standard scanone permutation tests might be overly conservative.

Say we expect there to be k = 1 QTL (that causes differential expression). In this case, it may make sense to pull out the 2nd highest permutation peak, instead of the highest one.

I had no problem writing a function that permutes the phenotype into a matrix, then pulls out the kth+1 highest peaks for each permuted trait. However, I am having trouble with more complicated situations, such as n covar > 0 or perm.strata != NULL.

Another approach would be to implement GWERk in scanone... I think it might be pretty easy to alter the  scanone.perm.engine code as follows:
standard perms:
res[i,] <- apply(tem[,-(1:2),drop=FALSE], 2, max, na.rm=TRUE)

GWERk perms:
res[i,] <- apply(tem[,-(1:2),drop=FALSE], 2, function(x) {
> m<-tapply(x,tem$chr,max, na.rm=TRUE) # get the maximum LOD scores / chromosome
> m[order(-m)][k+1] # get the kth + 1 highest lod peak
})

My question is, do you think this is an appropriate adjustment?
Thanks,
John

John T. Lovell
University of Texas at Austin

messages.body_plain:
You could just update the list of cofactors, which is simply a vector of 1's and 0's, specifying which markers should be included as cofactor.

If this doesn't work (since MQM does have some issues with single marker chromosomes (e.g. unlinked markers), I would just compensate/ adjust the phenotype for the marker in question, and then use the adjusted phenotype for further (multiple) QTL mapping
